blocks.title: Affine shifts
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:aff label="sec:aff"}

As mentioned above, the R-charge used in the index does not need to coincide with the R-charge that appears in the superconformal algebra. We can take $R$ to be any R-symmetry charge. If we redefine the R-charge by a flavor symmetry, then different choices are related by $R \to R -\alpha_e \cdot e$ for some vector $\alpha_e$. Under such a shift, the index varies accordingly as

$$\mathcal{I}_\mathcal{T}(m,e;q) \to q^{-\tfrac{1}{2} \alpha_e \cdot e} \mathcal{I}_\mathcal{T}(m,e;q)\,.$$

A discrete symmetry
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:kappa label="sec:kappa"}

We could define standard discrete symmetries $C$, $P$, and $T$ acting on theories $\mathcal{T}$ and their indices, though in general the 3d SCFT's in class $\mathcal{R}$ will not be invariant under any of these "symmetries" alone. blocks.title: The tetrahedron index
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:T1 label="sec:T1"}

The basic building block used to construct the theory $T_M$ for any 3-manifold $M$ is the theory $T_\Delta$ associated to a single ideal tetrahedron. More precisely, we should call the theory

$$T_{\Delta,\Pi_Z}\,, \label{tetthy}$$

since it depends on a polarization for the boundary of the tetrahedron. As discussed in Sections 2 and 4 of [@DGG], we make a specific choice of polarization $\Pi_Z$ (see also Section [\[sec:tetdiff\]](#sec:tetdiff){reference-type="ref" reference="sec:tetdiff"} below). blocks.title: Parity and symmetry
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:tetkappa label="sec:tetkappa"}

Several identities satisfied by the tetrahedron index can be understood via discrete symmetries acting on $T_\Delta$. Let's first consider the action of parity $\mathbf{P}$ on $T_\Delta$. In is not an exact symmetry because it inverts the sign of the Chern-Simons level, from $k=-\tfrac12$ to $k=\tfrac12$. However, this can be compensated for by subtracting a Chern-Simons term, *i.e.* applying $T^{-1}\in Sp(2,{\mathbb Z})$. blocks.title: Triality
Difference equations
The index of TM
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:TM label="sec:TM"}

Several copies of the tetrahedron theory $T_\Delta$ can be appropriately combined to construct an $\mathcal{N}=2$ SCFT associated to any oriented 3-manifold $M$ that admits an ideal triangulation. The gluing rules for $T_\Delta$ theories, described in [@DGG], immediately translate to a simple, combinatorial prescription for calculating the supersymmetric index $\mathcal{I}_M \equiv \mathcal{I}_{T_M}$ of $T_M$ on $S^2\times S^1$. blocks.title: Gluing rules
The bipyramid
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:bip label="sec:bip"}

As a simple but crucial example of a nontrivial 3-manifold, let us take $M$ to be the bipyramid, shown in the center of Figure [1](#fig:bip){reference-type="ref" reference="fig:bip"}. The bipyramid can be decomposed into either 2 or 3 tetrahedra, leading to two different UV descriptions of the theory $T_M$. It was shown in [@DGG] that, with an appropriate polarization, the gluing of two tetrahedra produces $N_f=1$ SQED, while the gluing of three tetrahedra produces the so-called XYZ model, a theory of three chiral multiplets coupled by a cubic superpotential. blocks.title: Some knot complements
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:knots label="sec:knots"}

A well-studied class of 3-manifolds are the complements of knots in the 3-sphere. One forms a knot complement $M_K$ by slightly thickening a knot $K\in S^3$ into a solid torus $N_K$, and then cutting it out,

$$M_K = S^3\backslash N_K\,.$$

With the single exception of the unknot complement, all knot complements seem to admit

[^1]

ideal triangulations that can be used to define the index $\mathcal{I}_{M_K}$, a topological invariant of $M_K$.

Tentacles and vacua
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:tent label="sec:tent"}

Some interesting physical consequences of the difference equations [\[Meqs\]](#Meqs){reference-type="eqref" reference="Meqs"} result from the fact that they control the behavior of the index at large charges $(m,e)$, in a fairly simple manner. There are actually two ways to send $m$ and/or $e$ to infinity: we can either keep $|q|<1$ fixed, or simultaneously send $m\to \infty$ and $q\to 1$ ($\hbar\to 0$) so that $q^m$ stays fixed. blocks.title: Mutation invariance from gauge theory
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:mutant label="sec:mutant"}

In this section, we begin to test the strength of the index as a topological invariant of 3-manifolds --- *i.e.* its ability to distinguish 3-manifolds from one another. We will specialize to the case of knot complements $M$, either in $S^3$ or in some closed 3-manifold $\overline M$, and consider the operation of mutation [@Conway-mutation]. blocks.title: Boundary conditions for hypermultiplets
blocks.content:
So far, we have considered $U(1)^N$ vector multiplets coupled to a boundary theory $T_M$. Generically, the 4d theories $T[\partial M]$ arising from a geodesic boundary $M$ will also involve hypermultiplet matter, which leads to further interesting observations in our 3d/4d setup.

A theory of a single hypermultiplet has two natural classes of boundary conditions. blocks.title: Non-abelian line defects
blocks.content:
There are natural ways to use the three-dimensional theories $T_M$ to define domain walls in the UV for four-dimensional ${\cal N}=2$ $SU(2)$ gauge theories. blocks.title: The index as SL(2,C) Chern-Simons theory
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:CS label="sec:CS"}

Throughout the preceding sections, there have been various hints that the index $\mathcal{I}_M(m,e;q)$ of a theory $T_M$ may have some relation to complex Chern-Simons theory on $M$ itself, *i.e.* Chern-Simons theory with complex gauge group $SL(2,{\mathbb C})$. blocks.content:
Tentacles and diﬀerence equations
In this appendix, we seek to motivate the relation between tentacles of a classical amoeba of
LM and “linear growth” in the index, as discussed in Section 4.6. We show how these two
phenomena are connected via quantized diﬀerence equations ˆLMIM = 0. Our argument is
heuristic, but indicates a path toward a more rigorous proof, given further information about
quantization and/or indices.
